summary: Describes use cases and required LDP Downstream-on-Demand label advertisement procedures for Seamless MPLS, where small access devices cannot hold much state. It also adds an optional TLV type to the LDP Label Request message.

eli5.summary: Small devices ask for directions only when needed instead of memorizing every road in the country.

subtitle: Letting small access routers ask for MPLS labels only when they need them.

tldr.problem: Access nodes in a large Seamless MPLS network have limited memory and compute, but normal LDP Downstream Unsolicited advertises labels for all valid routes.
tldr.mechanism: Access nodes use LDP Downstream-on-Demand with ordered control and liberal retention, requesting labels only for the routes they need. The RFC also defines an optional Queue Request TLV so a request waits for a missing route.
tldr.outcome: Access devices hold only the labels their services require, with failures propagated and alternates pre-programmed for fast repair.

today: RFC 7032 is a Proposed Standard from October 2013 and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It builds on LDP as specified in RFC 5036.

sections.title: Why Access Nodes Need On-Demand Labels
sections.content:
Seamless MPLS lets one IP/MPLS network scale across core, metro and access parts. Access devices are numerous, sit at the edge of the topology, and have limited compute and memory, which limits the state they can hold.

In access topologies a default route towards the aggregation nodes (AGNs) is often enough for IP. MPLS forwarding state is a different matter. Normal LDP Downstream Unsolicited (DU) advertisements (RFC 5036) hand out labels for all valid routes, which the RFC sees as inadequate for access nodes (ANs). Filters on DU are not seen as a suitable tool for any-to-any AN-driven connectivity. The document therefore describes a "subscription model" built on standard LDP Downstream-on-Demand (DoD), so only required labels are requested, provided and installed. It applies to IPv4 and IPv6, and covers unicast only; multicast is left for further study.
sections.eli5: A small device cannot carry a giant map. It asks for just the directions to the places it actually goes.

sections.title: Reference Access Topologies
sections.content:
The reference network has an access network attached to AGN1x nodes, an aggregation domain, and a core, all one MPLS network. The AGNs act as access area border routers (access ABRs).

With static routing, the topologies are named [I1], [I], [V], [U2] and [Y]: for example [V] is a single AN dual-homed to two AGNs, and [Y] is a chain of ANs reaching two AGNs. Each AN gets a static default route towards the AGNs and routes for the loopbacks it needs. With an access IGP, the topologies are [U], a chain of ANs in an open ring dual-homed to two AGNs, and [Y]. The AGNs advertise a default route into the access IGP, and ANs advertise their loopbacks.

In all cases ANs support Inter-area LDP (RFC 5283) so the default route can match LDP FECs advertised by the AGNs and other ANs. Parallel ECMP or L2 LAG links can be used between nodes.
sections.eli5: Small devices hang off bigger ones in simple shapes like chains and rings. The bigger devices connect them to the rest of the network.

sections.title: Use Cases from Setup to Failure
sections.content:
At initial setup an AN has no services and can still request labels for loopbacks of other nodes. An upstream node sends a Label Request for a configured static route that has an LDP DoD request policy. The downstream node answers with a label mapping if the route is in its RIB and it has a valid label from its own downstream neighbour (or is the egress). Otherwise it forwards the request on. Requests also go to alternate next hops to support ECMP and IPFRR LFA local repair (RFC 5286). On the network side AGNs can use BGP labeled IP routes (RFC 3107).

For service provisioning the RFC uses two examples, a pseudowire (RFC 4447) and a BGP/MPLS IP VPN (RFC 4364). Either way the AN needs LDP DoD labels for the destination /32 and its own loopback, and the DoD operation is service agnostic. When a service is removed, a label requested because of the service is released, but a label requested by a static /32 route with a request policy is retained.

For failures, neighbours remove routes and labels and send Label Withdraw upstream, and nodes switch to ECMP or alternate paths where they exist. The RFC also asks for LDP session protection and, with an access IGP, IGP-LDP synchronization. If an AGN loses network reachability it withdraws labels for the affected /32 FECs, and if it is isolated it stops advertising the default route into the access IGP.
sections.eli5: When a new service starts, the device asks for the directions it needs. When a road breaks, neighbours tell each other and switch to another road.

sections.title: LDP DoD Procedures
sections.content:
This section does not update RFC 5036. Labels are assigned by the downstream LSR and signalled to the upstream LSR. Access LSRs use DoD with ordered label distribution control, which lets a label binding failure propagate through the access topology, and liberal label retention, which allows labels for alternate next hops to be pre-programmed. The RFC notes that with an access IGP and no LFA, labels for a new next hop are only requested after IGP convergence, adding delay.

To open a session, an LSR proposes DoD by setting the "A" value to 1 in the Common Session Parameters TLV of the Initialization message. If an LSR that supports only DoD is offered DU, it sends a Notification "Session Rejected/Parameters Advertisement Mode" and closes the session. An active LSR retries immediately, then follows the exponential backoff of RFC 5036 starting at 15 seconds up to a maximum of 2 minutes. PWE3 FECs on the same session still use DU as in RFC 4447.

Requests are triggered by a /32 static route with a DoD request policy, by a configured service, or by a link coming up. A downstream node replies with a non-null label if it has one from the next-next-hop (asking onward if needed), or, on an ABR, if the best route is a BGP labeled route. It may reply with explicit-null or implicit-null if it is the egress, or send a "No Route" notification, which triggers a retry with exponential backoff. A duplicate request must not be sent, and a Label Abort is sent if the route or policy goes away before the mapping arrives.

A downstream node sends Label Withdraw when its label is no longer valid, for example when the BGP route or IGP route is withdrawn, the session is lost, or policy blocks the export. The upstream node answers with Label Release and re-requests if it still needs the label. For next-hop changes the downstream node first tries to converge locally and withdraws only if no mapping arrives. An upstream node also releases a label if it receives an unsolicited mapping on a DoD session.
sections.eli5: Devices ask for labels, get answers, and say so when a label is no longer needed. If a road disappears, the news travels back to whoever was using it.

sections.title: The Queue Request TLV
sections.content:
If a route is missing when a Label Request arrives, the downstream LSR sends "No Route" and the requester backs off, which can leave a long wait after the route returns. The RFC defines a new optional parameter for the Label Request message, the Queue Request TLV, with type 0x0971 and length 0x00. Its U-bit is 1 and its F-bit is 0. Implementing it is a SHOULD if fast-up convergence is desired.

The upstream LSR adds the TLV to ask the downstream LSR to queue the request. A supporting downstream LSR replies with a label mapping as soon as the route is available, and sends no "No Route" meanwhile. The upstream LSR does not retry. To cancel, it sends a Label Abort Request and gets a Label Request Aborted notification. A downstream LSR that does not understand the TLV ignores it and sends "No Route", so the upstream LSR falls back to exponential backoff, which keeps the extension backward compatible.

IANA assigned TLV type 0x0971 in the LDP "TLV Type Name Space" registry for the Queue Request TLV.
sections.eli5: Instead of being told to come back later, the helper writes your request on a list and answers when it has the information.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
LDP DoD in access is subject to the same threats as any LDP deployment, so baseline measures from RFC 5036 and the MPLS security framework are recommended. Some access nodes sit in street cabinets, so designers must also consider physical security.

DoD is request driven and upstream LSRs do not accept unsolicited label mappings, which limits injection by a third party and lets the ABR control what each access LSR can request. With static access routes a compromised node cannot influence ABR routing. With an access IGP, a compromised leaf has no adverse effect, a compromised transit node can only attract traffic for nodes upstream of it, and network FEC stealing is prevented by preferring BGP labeled routes over access IGP routes.

For the control plane, LDP sessions should only be set up with trusted peers. Spoofed Hellos can be reduced with the RFC 5036 guidelines and an optional Cryptographic Authentication TLV, and session spoofing by using the TCP Authentication Option rather than MD5.
sections.eli5: Because devices only accept answers to questions they asked, a stranger cannot slip them fake directions.

fields.desc: Unknown TLV bit; 1, so a receiver that does not know the TLV ignores it.
